newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Some Slovak banks call on NBS to ease up.
newsitem.headline: Some Slovak banks call on NBS to ease up.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) says it will maintain its current tight monetary policy, but some commercial banks are calling for more relaxed policies to help foster economic growth.

Several senior Slovak bankers have questioned whether the NBS should use the M2 measure of money supply, comprising currency in circulation, deposits and savings, as strictly as it does to determine monetary policy.
They say Slovakia's deeply under-capitalised economy needs further financial injections to continue reforms.

"In our opinion the M2 (rate) as a basic criterion for assesing monetary development should not be applied as strictly here as in fully developed market economies," Jan Gabriel, President of the largest commercial bank VUB, told the country's leading businessmen at a seminar last week.
The NBS has rejected calls to stop using the M2 benchmark, saying that if it did, it would be impossible to keep inflation within its target range.
"Our target is to keep the currency stable and maintain the so-far favourable development of inflation," Peter Sevcovic, head of the NBS Monetary policy departent, told Reuters.
"You can call it strict but it has has never been restrictive," Sevcovic said.
He added that the fact that M2 has so far always exceeded GDP growth was clear evidence of a non-restrictive policy.

Slovak inflation, still one of the lowest rates in post-communist Europe, rose 0.7 percent in October, putting prices 5.3 percent higher year-on-year. The official forecasts for next year's inflation foresee a rate of under six percent.
Gabriel said he expected M2 growth to be well under the NBS target of 11.6 percent this year, even though the central bank fears it will be higher than that as it is currently at over 18 percent.
Gabriel saw no problem in faster credit expansion, which he forecasted to significantly exceed the NBS target of 7.2 percent year-on-year increase.
"There is no such direct connection (between these factors) as in market economies, since our economy is under-capitalised and needs money to progress in reforms," Gabriel said.
"Of course there is a clear connection between credit expansion, money supply growth and inflation... We cannot ease the policy and let inflation jump, for example, to 12 percent."
NBS vice-governor Marian Jusko last week said M2 growth in the first ten months of the year was at "around" 18 percent year-on-year, down from 19 percent in September.

The overall volume of credits continued to rise in September by some 1.3 billion crowns ($48.69 million), putting the total volume at 355.4 billion as of September 30 - a 19.2 percent increase year-on-year. -- Bratislava Newsroom, 42-7-563-3687
